Taken together, owners of rent-controlled or subsidized portfolios should treat unresolved code violations as rapidly compounding legal exposure rather than routine administrative matters, verify that every habitability representation made to an agency or lender matches the property's actual condition, and recognize that courts are willing to order an operational takeover well before a case reaches final judgment, making early remediation and transparent recordkeeping the far more defensible course.
live-076: A CMBS special servicer has filed suit to foreclose on a two-floor retail condominium at the base of a 21-story tower on Chicago's State Street, the latest sign that loan maturity defaults continue to work through the Loop's distressed commercial debt even in property types that once looked more resilient than office. Rialto Capital Advisors, acting as special servicer for a securitized commercial mortgage loan trust, filed the foreclosure action on April 1, 2026 in the Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois, against Jenel Management Corp. and affiliated Jenel Real Estate entities, the New York-based landlord that owns the roughly 20,211-square-foot retail condominium occupying the first two floors of the tower at 36 South State Street, at the corner of State and Monroe. The dispute traces back to a 2018 transaction in which Jenel purchased the retail condominium from Thor Equities, the New York investment firm led by Joe Sitt, for approximately $26 million, assuming roughly $16.8 million of existing mortgage debt in the process. According to Rialto's complaint, that loan reached its scheduled maturity date and went unpaid, triggering the default now at issue. Rialto's filing puts the total amount owed at approximately $17.7 million, reflecting not just the original principal balance but also default interest, late fees, and liquidation costs that accrue once a CMBS loan transfers to special servicing and enforcement begins. Cook County's circuit court has scheduled a hearing in the matter for September 28, 2026, an early test of how quickly the foreclosure can proceed and whether Jenel intends to contest the default or negotiate a resolution before judgment. The case is procedurally a straightforward commercial mortgage foreclosure, but its context matters more than its mechanics. Retail condominiums at high-profile downtown corners were, for much of the past decade, treated as a relatively defensive CRE asset class: unlike office towers grappling with a structural shift toward remote and hybrid work, ground-floor retail in a dense urban core depends primarily on foot traffic and tenancy rather than corporate space decisions. The State Street corridor has nonetheless weathered its own version of the broader Loop's struggles, and financing underwritten against pre-pandemic rent and occupancy assumptions is increasingly colliding with maturities in a materially higher interest-rate environment, pushing otherwise performing properties into technical default simply because the maturity balloon cannot be refinanced on comparable terms. For landlords and lenders alike, the dispute is a reminder that special servicers move deliberately once a maturity default occurs. CMBS pooling and servicing agreements generally require the servicer to act in the collective interest of certificate holders, which in practice means pursuing foreclosure, receivership, or a negotiated workout on a timeline dictated by the trust's governing documents rather than by any particular borrower's preferences. A borrower facing an approaching maturity wall has meaningfully more leverage before a default occurs and a loan transfers to special servicing than after a servicer has already filed suit, at which point the practical range of outcomes narrows toward a pressured forbearance, a receivership that displaces the borrower from day-to-day control, or a foreclosure sale that extinguishes the borrower's equity entirely. Owners and lenders active in downtown Chicago should treat this filing as a data point rather than an isolated incident: a loan secured by a well-located, seemingly stable retail asset can still default on maturity without any precipitating tenant bankruptcy or occupancy collapse, simply because 2018-vintage debt-service coverage and loan-to-value assumptions no longer clear today's underwriting bar. Commercial borrowers with loans approaching maturity, particularly those originated at pre-2022 rate and valuation assumptions, should engage lenders on extension or refinancing terms well before the maturity date rather than waiting for a monetary default to force the conversation, and buyers evaluating distressed or maturing CRE debt in the Loop should model maturity risk independently of a property's clean operating history, since strong performance to date is no longer sufficient assurance that a loan will refinance on its own terms.
live-077: A Massachusetts judge has dismantled an eleventh-hour attempt to hold up the $2.1 billion take-private acquisition of Plymouth Industrial REIT, Inc., ruling that a real estate advisory firm's claim to a roughly $20 million success fee on the deal could not proceed because the firm was acting as an unregistered securities broker when it says it earned that fee. The ruling, issued January 20, 2026 by Justice Kenneth W. Salinger in the Business Litigation Session of Suffolk County Superior Court, denied plaintiff Redimere Advisors LLC's emergency motion for a preliminary injunction and dismissed all of its claims against Plymouth, resolving a dispute that had briefly threatened to complicate the merger's closing. Plymouth Industrial REIT, a publicly traded industrial REIT, agreed to be acquired by an investor group led by Makarora Management LP together with funds affiliated with Ares Alternative Credit in an all-cash transaction valuing the company at $22.00 per share, or approximately $2.1 billion. Redimere Advisors, which describes itself as a real estate advisory and brokerage firm, claimed it had orally agreed with Plymouth to earn a 2% success fee, roughly $20 million on a deal of this size, in exchange for introducing Plymouth to the Makarora and Ares buyer group and assisting in bringing the take-private transaction to a close. Plymouth countered that its only written engagement with Redimere, a letter agreement dated November 28, 2022, covered a narrower scope of equity-financing work and did not extend to the merger. When Plymouth declined to pay the claimed fee, Redimere sued and sought an emergency injunction that would have blocked the merger from closing, or alternatively diverted roughly $60 million of the merger proceeds into escrow with a third-party trustee pending resolution of its claims. Justice Salinger's ruling disposed of the case on two independent grounds, either of which would likely have been sufficient on its own. First, the court found that the written 2022 engagement letter did not cover the take-private transaction with Makarora and Ares, meaning Plymouth had no contractual obligation to pay Redimere a fee on that deal regardless of what role Redimere may have played in facilitating it. Second, and more consequentially for the broader industry, the court held that any oral agreement to pay Redimere a transaction-based success fee was unenforceable because Redimere was acting as an unregistered broker in connection with a securities transaction, in violation of the registration requirements of the federal Securities Exchange Act. Because the merger involved the sale of Plymouth's publicly traded securities rather than a direct asset sale, arranging or facilitating that transaction for a transaction-based fee is activity federal securities law reserves to registered broker-dealers, and an unregistered firm generally cannot use the courts to enforce a fee arrangement premised on having performed that function. The decision carries implications well beyond this single dispute. Real estate advisory firms, deal originators, and finders frequently operate on the understanding that a handshake or email exchange promising a percentage-based fee for introducing a buyer is enforceable so long as the introduction leads to a closed transaction. Where the underlying transaction is structured as a stock or securities deal, as REIT take-privates and public company mergers generally are, that assumption can be wrong as a matter of law regardless of the equities of who actually brought the parties together, since the registration requirement exists precisely to ensure that intermediaries facilitating securities transactions are subject to regulatory oversight. For REITs and other public companies pursuing M&A or take-private transactions, the case also illustrates how courts weigh eleventh-hour injunction requests aimed at merger proceeds. Judges are generally reluctant to freeze deal proceeds or delay a closing based on a contested fee claim where the underlying contractual and regulatory defenses are strong enough to be resolved at the motion stage. Redimere's decision to seek both an injunction against the closing and, alternatively, an escrow of tens of millions of dollars reflects a litigation strategy that depends on a court being willing to disrupt a transaction's timeline even where the underlying claim is legally shaky, and here that strategy failed on both fronts. REITs and other public real estate companies negotiating with outside advisors, brokers, or deal originators should ensure written engagement letters clearly define the scope of covered transactions, since ambiguity about whether a later, larger deal falls within an earlier engagement is exactly the kind of gap that generates litigation. Any intermediary expecting to earn a transaction-based fee on a securities deal should confirm it is either a registered broker-dealer or that its role and compensation fit within an available exemption before assuming an oral fee arrangement will be enforceable, and companies facing a late fee dispute as a deal approaches closing should recognize that courts are generally unwilling to freeze merger proceeds absent a strong showing on the merits, which limits the practical leverage such claims carry even on an emergency basis.
live-078: A proposed class action over noise from a cryptocurrency-mining and artificial-intelligence data center in rural Cherokee County, North Carolina has turned into a fight over which court gets to hear it, in a dispute that will help define how commercial data-center operators and their neighbors litigate nuisance claims as the industry's physical footprint keeps expanding into residential and rural areas. Residents Judith Stines and William Huffman sued PrimeBlock Operations, LLC, a California-based bitcoin-mining company, along with affiliated entities Exponential Digital LLC and Innotech Z Inc., alleging the roughly three-acre facility near Harshaw Road outside Murphy has generated continuous, unabated noise from its servers, generators, and industrial cooling systems since it began operating in September 2021. According to the complaint, sound-level readings near affected properties have ranged from 55 to 85 decibels depending on weather conditions, and neighbors describe the noise not primarily by its volume but by its constancy — one resident likened it to a small jet that never leaves. Stines and Huffman are seeking to represent a class of property owners and residents within a two-mile radius of the facility, a group the complaint estimates at nearly 1,000 people, on the theory that the defendants have declined to invest in basic noise-abatement measures despite years of documented complaints. The case was removed from state court to the U.S. District Court for the Western District of North Carolina, and the plaintiffs have since moved to send it back, arguing on September 2, 2026 that the damages actually at stake fall short of the amount-in-controversy threshold required to keep a proposed class action in federal court under the Class Action Fairness Act. That threshold fight is not a technicality so much as a proxy battle over venue advantage: state courts in rural counties are often viewed as more receptive to local nuisance and property-value claims, while federal court offers a defendant more predictable procedural rules and, in a CAFA-eligible case, more rigorous scrutiny of aggregate class damages before certification. How a plaintiff frames its damages ask at the outset of a nuisance class action can therefore be less about maximizing recovery and more about controlling where the case gets decided. The dispute also highlights a gap between regulatory compliance and common-law liability that matters well beyond this one facility. Murphy and other municipalities that have seen mining or data-center noise complaints have responded by adopting new local noise ordinances, but satisfying a decibel limit measured at a property line does not resolve whether an operation's ongoing noise substantially and unreasonably interferes with a neighbor's use and enjoyment of their own property under common-law nuisance doctrine. A facility can be fully compliant with an applicable ordinance and still face a viable nuisance claim, because the two legal standards ask different questions and are enforced through entirely different mechanisms — one through code enforcement, the other through private civil litigation. For developers, operators, and lenders financing data centers, crypto-mining facilities, and similar high-density industrial infrastructure, the case is a reminder that community noise complaints sustained over several years can mature into class-scale civil exposure well before any regulator acts, and that removal to federal court is a strategic choice with real downside if a remand motion succeeds after months of litigation have already been spent contesting the forum rather than the merits. Site-selection and community-relations diligence for this asset class increasingly needs to account for nuisance litigation risk with the same rigor traditionally reserved for zoning and permitting review.
live-079: A Sacramento County Superior Court judge has cleared the way for a neighboring business owner to pursue negligence, fraud, and punitive-damages claims against the developer and contractors behind the Mirasol Village redevelopment, in a case testing how far liability for legacy soil contamination can travel beyond a project's own boundaries. Betty Mitchell operated an indoor cannabis cultivation company, Liveade Wellness Inc., near the site of Mirasol Village, the master-planned redevelopment of the former Twin Rivers public housing project in Sacramento's River District. Mitchell alleges her cultivation operation tested positive for chlordane, a synthetic pesticide the federal government banned in 1988, despite the fact that she says the chemical was never used, stored, or introduced anywhere on her own property. Mirasol Village is being developed by McCormack Baron Salazar, Inc., a national affordable-housing developer, together with general contractor A. Teichert & Son, Inc. and site contractor Midstate Construction Corporation. The contamination history at the site predates the current dispute: a March 4, 2020 letter from the California Department of Toxic Substances Control identified organochlorine pesticides, including chlordane, as chemicals of concern at the property and called for additional environmental investigation. Mitchell's complaint, filed in April 2025, alleges that dust generated during the redevelopment's construction activity carried that legacy contamination beyond the project boundary and into her nearby facility, ultimately rendering her cultivation operation's product unsellable and destroying a business she says she had invested nearly $1 million to build. What distinguishes this case from a routine construction-dust complaint is which claims survived the defendants' effort to dismiss it. A negligence theory, alleging inadequate dust and soil containment during construction, is a familiar fact pattern in environmental liability litigation involving redevelopment sites. Judge Sueyoshi's rulings, however, also allowed Mitchell's fraud and punitive-damages claims to proceed, meaning the court found she had pled facts capable of supporting an inference of conduct beyond ordinary carelessness. Punitive damages against a development team require a considerably higher showing — something closer to conscious disregard of a known risk — and a court's willingness to let such a claim clear the pleading stage is itself a meaningful signal about how the underlying facts are being read at this early stage. The case sits at the intersection of two problems increasingly common as cities redevelop aging public housing, industrial, and agricultural parcels: legacy contamination that predates current ownership by decades, and the reality that construction dust and disturbed soil do not respect parcel lines. Developers typically manage their own on-site environmental exposure through Phase I/II assessments, regulatory oversight agreements, and contractual risk allocation with their construction team. Managing liability to an unrelated, neighboring business with no contractual relationship to the project at all is a different and less familiar problem, and this case puts it squarely at issue. The prior DTSC notice is likely to loom large as the case proceeds. Because regulators had already flagged organochlorine pesticides as a chemical of concern at the site years before construction began, Mitchell's claims are positioned to argue the defendants had specific, documented notice of the contamination risk rather than encountering it as a surprise during construction — a fact pattern that tends to strengthen a negligence claim and can support the kind of knowing-disregard theory a punitive-damages claim requires.
live-080: Commercial property owners who buy surplus lines coverage rarely stop to ask what happens if their policy is split across a dozen different insurers, some domestic and some overseas, and a hurricane forces a coverage fight. On September 3, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit answered that question for Louisiana, holding that an arbitration clause in a surplus lines commercial property policy is unenforceable against the domestic insurers on the policy even though the identical clause remains enforceable against the foreign insurers subscribing to the very same contract. The underlying facts are unremarkable for coastal Louisiana. Transportation Consultants, Inc. owned commercial property insured under a surplus lines policy subscribed by nine domestic insurance companies and two foreign underwriters at Lloyd's of London. The policy contained a broad arbitration clause covering virtually any disagreement over the insurance, along with a contract allocation endorsement treating the policy as a series of separate bilateral contracts between the policyholder and each individual subscribing insurer rather than as one contract among many co-insurers. When Hurricane Ida damaged the insured property, a coverage dispute followed, and Transportation Consultants sued all eleven insurers together in Louisiana state court. The insurers removed the case to the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana, invoking the Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards as the basis for federal jurisdiction given the Lloyd's syndicates' involvement. The district court initially granted the insurers' motion to compel arbitration across the board and stayed the entire case, then reversed course on reconsideration as to the nine domestic insurers, holding that Louisiana Revised Statutes 22:868, which generally voids policy provisions depriving Louisiana courts of jurisdiction over suits against an insurer, barred enforcement of the arbitration clause against insurers domiciled in the United States. The court lifted the litigation stay for those nine defendants while leaving the arbitration order intact for the two Lloyd's underwriters, whose contracts fell within the Convention's separate, preemptive framework for international arbitration agreements. On appeal, the Fifth Circuit affirmed that split result. Following its own recent precedents in Town of Vinton v. Indian Harbor Insurance Co. and Crescent City Surgical Operating Co. v. Interstate Fire & Casualty Co., the panel held that the Convention's preemptive reach over arbitration agreements extends only to the contracts between the policyholder and the foreign insurers, not to the parallel contracts, created by the same policy language and contract allocation endorsement, between the policyholder and the domestic insurers. Because those domestic contracts are governed by ordinary Louisiana law rather than the Convention, Section 22:868's anti-arbitration rule applies to them in full force. The court also rejected the domestic insurers' fallback argument that equitable estoppel should let them ride along with the enforceable arbitration obligations of their foreign co-subscribers simply because all eleven insurers signed the same policy form. The practical significance for commercial real estate owners and their brokers is direct: any surplus lines program covering Louisiana property that mixes domestic and foreign capacity now creates two separate dispute-resolution tracks that diverge the moment a claim is contested, one heading to court against the domestic carriers and one heading to arbitration against the foreign carriers, even though the underlying coverage grant and facts are identical. Sophisticated insureds should press their brokers at the placement stage for clarity on which subscribing markets are domestic versus foreign, since that distinction can otherwise sit unnoticed as boilerplate until a storm turns it into a jurisdictional battleground, and should budget for the real cost of potentially prosecuting the same coverage theory in two forums at once rather than assuming a single track will resolve the whole dispute.
live-081: A fraud lawsuit filed in Johnson County, Kansas has become the legal centerpiece of one of 2026's more dramatic commercial real estate collapses: the unraveling of Vesta Realty and Vesta Capital, a Tulsa-based multifamily platform that at its peak controlled roughly 39 apartment properties and nearly 10,000 units across Oklahoma, Kansas, and Arkansas, valued at close to $1 billion. The case, captioned Vesta Capital, LLC, et al. v. Marc Kulick, et al. and pending before Judge Joann Woltman in the Tenth Judicial District, accuses Kulick, the platform's founder and chief executive, of diverting more than $37 million in investor and company funds for personal use while concealing the portfolio's deteriorating finances from the investors who capitalized it. The suit was brought by Josef Loeffler, a longtime business partner who says he was responsible for raising capital for the venture while Kulick, as sole manager, retained exclusive control over the properties' books, bank accounts, and cash management. According to the complaint, Kulick cultivated a public image as a philanthropist and savvy operator even as the portfolio slid toward insolvency, allegedly moving cash between affiliated entities to mask shortfalls, sidestepping the accounting controls investors had been promised, and deflecting scrutiny with what the pleading describes as blandishments, bluster, and bullying. The complaint further alleges Kulick liquidated at least one property without distributing proceeds to investors, took out additional loans without authorization, and directed company funds toward more than $37 million in personal credit card payments, car loans, and gambling debts. The litigation carries an unusual procedural wrinkle. Loeffler and Kulick had structured at least part of their arrangement as a heter iska, a rabbinical financing instrument that recasts what would otherwise be an interest-bearing loan as a profit-sharing investment so as to comply with Jewish law's prohibition on charging interest between coreligionists. When Loeffler moved to enforce his rights in Kansas state court, Kulick argued the dispute belonged before a beis din, a rabbinical tribunal, rather than a secular judge. Loeffler's counsel countered that Kulick had already been summoned before religious authorities, refused to appear, and was subsequently issued a heter arko'os, effectively a religious-law permission slip authorizing recourse to civil court, making his belated invocation of the arbitration clause remarkable for its audacity. The motion to dismiss remains pending. While the Kansas fraud suit works through Judge Woltman's docket, Vesta's broader collapse has spilled into courts and receiverships across two more states. In Oklahoma County, lenders on the 272-unit Drexel Flats complex in southwest Oklahoma City moved to foreclose after Vesta-affiliated borrowers failed to turn over rents on a matured loan carrying roughly $28 million to $30 million in outstanding debt; a state court judge ordered Vesta removed as property manager and a receiver installed after tenants endured months of unpaid utility bills and overflowing trash service, though Vesta briefly regained control of the property on appeal before the receivership dispute returned to the docket. Separately, Efraim Diveroli, the former arms dealer whose exploits inspired the film War Dogs, extended Kulick a series of loans carrying reported interest rates compounding at extraordinary annualized levels, then moved through his firm, YSA Investments 1, LLC, to seize roughly two dozen Vesta-affiliated properties via deeds in lieu of foreclosure after Kulick defaulted. That takeover fight took its own dramatic turn on July 28, 2026, when YSA itself filed for Chapter 11 protection in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware, with a Chapter 11 trustee appointed within minutes of the filing to sort out competing claims to the disputed properties. For commercial real estate investors, lenders, and joint-venture partners, the Vesta saga is ultimately a governance story rather than a market-cycle story: a sponsor with sole, unchecked authority over cash management, reinforced by financing structures like the heter iska that operate outside conventional secured-lending documentation, can obscure a portfolio's true condition from capital partners for a surprisingly long time, particularly when growth is funded through complex intercompany transfers rather than transparent, audited distributions. The Oklahoma receivership actions also show how quickly deferred maintenance and unpaid municipal bills can escalate into a full change of control once a court concludes tenants are being harmed, while the entrance of a high-cost private lender willing to extend usurious-seeming credit to an already-distressed sponsor, only to end up in bankruptcy itself, is a reminder that rescue capital arriving after a sponsor is underwater rarely resolves a distressed situation cleanly; it typically just adds another layer of creditors and litigation to unwind. Investors negotiating LLC operating agreements would be well served to insist on independent audit rights, distribution waterfalls with real teeth, and forum-selection clauses that cannot later be weaponized to delay accountability, while lenders evaluating a distressed sponsor's rescue financing should scrutinize not just the collateral but the sponsor's demonstrated pattern of financial transparency before extending fresh credit into an already-troubled capital stack.
live-083: Copper Property CTL Pass Through Trust, the special-purpose entity created out of J.C. Penney's 2020 Chapter 11 reorganization to hold and eventually monetize the retailer's owned real estate, filed suit against Boston-based private equity firm Onyx Partners and its founder, Anton Melchionda, on August 25 in Massachusetts Superior Court, Suffolk County (Docket No. 2684CV02549-BLS1, Business Litigation Session). The complaint alleges that Onyx fraudulently induced Copper to sign a $947 million agreement to sell 119 former J.C. Penney store properties, spanning more than 15 million square feet across 35 states, by misrepresenting the state of its financing. Copper is seeking at least $150 million in damages. The filing is the latest turn in a deal that began with considerable promise. Onyx agreed roughly a year ago to acquire the portfolio outright, a transaction that would have allowed Copper's beneficiaries, largely the unsecured creditors left holding claims from J.C. Penney's bankruptcy, to realize value from real estate that had been slowly leased back and sold off in the years since the retailer's reorganization. The deal was expected to close in the fall of 2025 but slipped repeatedly, and by late December Onyx had missed what Copper treated as a final deadline. Copper walked away from the agreement, and within days Onyx sued first, filing its own breach-of-contract action in New York Supreme Court, New York County, on December 26 (OPLTD JCP LLC v. CTL Propco I LLC et al., Index No. 656690/2025) -- a different court from the one Copper's own suit landed in eight months later. That complaint accused Copper of acting in bad faith by quietly shopping the portfolio to other prospective buyers while negotiations with Onyx were still ongoing, and of blocking the closing by refusing to deliver a tenant estoppel certificate Onyx says the purchase agreement required. Onyx is seeking specific performance of the sale or, in the alternative, damages. Copper's new complaint answers that suit with an aggressive counter-narrative. Rather than accepting the characterization that it sabotaged the deal, Copper alleges that Onyx never had a realistic path to funding the purchase and that Melchionda and his firm repeatedly misrepresented the status of funding discussions with major financial institutions to make Onyx's financing look more certain than it actually was. In Copper's telling, the bid was a sham designed to lock up the portfolio and buy time, using leaked media coverage of the pending sale to its own advantage while quietly failing to line up the capital needed to perform. The complaint further alleges that the resulting uncertainty depressed the portfolio's value and left Copper unable to pursue alternative buyers on comparable terms once the Onyx deal fell apart. A separate, related skirmish is playing out over the $5 million deposit Onyx posted when the agreement was signed. Copper is holding $2 million of that deposit and is now seeking to claim the remaining $3 million held in escrow, a demand Onyx is contesting in the same litigation. For general counsel, asset managers, and institutional sellers, the dispute is a useful case study in how large, complex portfolio sales can unravel even after extensive due diligence and a signed agreement. Purchase-and-sale agreements involving distressed or bankruptcy-derived real estate frequently include closing conditions, such as tenant estoppel deliveries, financing contingencies, and deadline extensions, that create leverage for both sides once a deal begins to wobble; here, each party is now pointing to the other's conduct around those very mechanisms as the true cause of the collapse. Sellers negotiating large portfolio dispositions, particularly through litigation trusts or other creditor-recovery vehicles with fiduciary obligations to beneficiaries, should take note of how quickly a buyer's financing representations can become the central battleground once a deal falls through, and how naming a fund's principal individually, as Copper has done with Melchionda, can raise the stakes and complicate a defendant's settlement calculus. Buyers, in turn, should recognize that aggressive use of media narratives during a contested closing can later be cited as evidence of bad faith rather than legitimate deal pressure, and that both sides in a large bankruptcy-derived real estate sale should expect discovery into financing efforts and marketing conduct to dominate the early stages of litigation once a deal of this size collapses.
live-084: Dr. Bernard Feldman, a 72-year-old Des Moines gastroenterologist and private real estate lender, filed suit in Iowa District Court for Polk County on April 22 against Daniel Pettit, Rob Orton, and their jointly held entity, Mozart Properties, alleging breach of contract over a $850,000 loan extended in 2021 that was never repaid, with roughly $32,000 in accrued interest outstanding at the time of filing. The complaint is notable less for its dollar figure than for who it names: Orton, president of Orton Homes and chief executive of American Group LLC, an umbrella holding company for roughly twenty real estate-related businesses including RE/MAX Precision in Clive, had not previously been named as a defendant in the wave of litigation surrounding Pettit's finances. The lawsuit arrives amid a broader unraveling of Pettit's real estate empire that has drawn scrutiny from the FBI, the Johnston Police Department, and the Iowa Insurance Division. Pettit, the 43-year-old owner of Encompass Holdings and controlling partner in numerous limited liability companies, built a track record of substantial development deals in the Des Moines metro before running into significant financial distress after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. A subsequent probe found that Pettit allegedly owed roughly $70 million to banks, private investors, and former business partners, several of whom have already obtained judgments against him. Feldman himself previously won a separate judgment of nearly $9.3 million against Pettit after alleging fraud, fraudulent inducement, and misrepresentation in an earlier case. Pettit was later jailed in Polk County after spending more than a month evading a nationwide warrant, and additional investors, including a California couple, have since joined the line of creditors seeking to collect. The April complaint alleges that the 2021 loan to Pettit, Orton, and Mozart Properties was never repaid according to its terms, and pursues a straightforward breach-of-contract theory against all three defendants jointly. Unlike Feldman's earlier fraud-based judgment against Pettit individually, this suit's decision to add Orton and the jointly held Mozart Properties entity signals an effort by creditors to identify every solvent party connected to Pettit's dealings, rather than pursuing recovery solely against a developer whose assets and liquidity are already deeply compromised and subject to competing claims. For commercial real estate lenders and private investors who extend capital directly to developers outside of institutional bank financing, often on the strength of a personal relationship or a developer's track record rather than a fully diligenced credit underwriting process, the Pettit fallout illustrates both the appeal and the risk of that kind of private lending. Feldman's original loan, like many private notes extended to active local developers, appears to have been made on relatively informal terms relative to a bank facility, and the case underscores how difficult recovery becomes once a borrower's financial distress metastasizes across dozens of affiliated entities and multiple competing creditors. It also highlights a recovery strategy worth watching: when a primary borrower's own assets are insufficient or already encumbered by prior judgments, creditors increasingly look to co-obligors, guarantors, and business partners named on the same loan documents or jointly held entities, even when those parties have not previously faced public litigation over the underlying default. The practical lesson for real estate lenders, investors, and the counsel who structure private notes extends beyond this single case. Private lenders financing local developers should insist on clear, individually enforceable obligations from every principal and affiliated entity involved in a transaction, rather than relying on a single borrower's signature, since joint-and-several liability structured at origination becomes the difference between a recoverable claim and a worthless judgment once distress sets in. Diligence on a borrower's other outstanding obligations and pending litigation, not just their historical track record, has become essential in markets where a single overextended developer can generate cascading defaults across an entire network of investors, and once fraud or insolvency concerns surface around a borrower, co-investors and lenders should move quickly to identify and pursue all potentially solvent co-obligors before competing creditors exhaust the available recovery pool.
live-086: The U.S. Supreme Court agreed on June 29, 2026 to resolve a question that has quietly divided lower courts for years and that matters well beyond the pipeline industry: when a private company exercises the federal government's eminent domain power to condemn land, who pays the landowner's attorney's fees. In Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc., the Court will decide whether Section 7 of the Natural Gas Act displaces state fee-shifting statutes, like North Dakota's, that would otherwise let a successful condemnee recover the legal costs of fighting over just compensation. For any property owner, developer, or institutional landholder whose real estate sits along a proposed pipeline, transmission line, or other federally licensed infrastructure corridor, the outcome will help define the true cost of resisting a taking. The case traces back to 2018, when WBI Energy Transmission, Inc. exercised federal eminent domain authority under Natural Gas Act Section 7(h) to acquire pipeline easements across property owned by McKenzie County, North Dakota landowners Leonard and Denae Hoffmann, along with Randall Stevenson and Rocky Prestangen. The Natural Gas Act allows FERC-certificated pipeline companies to condemn private property for interstate gas transportation projects, but Section 7(h) itself does not directly address who bears the cost of litigating the condemnation, leaving that gap to be filled by state law under the federal condemnation procedure rules that ordinarily apply. North Dakota is among the states whose statutes entitle a landowner who successfully contests an eminent domain valuation to recover reasonable attorney's fees from the condemnor. The Hoffmanns and their co-petitioners reached a confidential settlement with WBI over the underlying just-compensation figure in 2021, but the parties kept litigating over the landowners' legal fees. A federal district court sided with the landowners, ordering WBI to pay roughly $380,000 in attorney's fees and related costs under North Dakota's fee-shifting statute. WBI appealed, and the Eighth Circuit reversed in the pipeline company's favor, holding that federal law displaces North Dakota's fee statute once a condemnation proceeds under the Natural Gas Act's federal eminent domain authority, leaving the landowners on the hook for their own legal expenses despite having successfully pressed their compensation claim and setting up the circuit-level conflict the Supreme Court has now agreed to resolve. The question presented turns on a distinctly technical but consequential point of federal preemption doctrine: whether Congress, in authorizing FERC-certificated pipelines to invoke federal eminent domain power under Section 7, meant to displace the state-law rules that would otherwise govern ancillary aspects of a condemnation proceeding, including fee-shifting, or whether those state-law rules continue to apply by default because Section 7 itself is silent on the subject. The landowners argue that federal condemnation procedure has long incorporated state law on exactly these kinds of questions absent a clear congressional directive to the contrary, while WBI contends that a uniform federal rule is necessary to avoid a patchwork of fee obligations that would vary pipeline-by-pipeline depending on which state's easement happens to be at issue. The case is expected to be argued during the Court's October 2026 Term, with a date to be set once briefing is complete. Because the question presented is framed narrowly around the Natural Gas Act, a ruling will speak directly to landowners facing pipeline condemnations, but the reasoning could reverberate further, since federal eminent domain authority is not unique to natural gas pipelines and also underlies certain transmission-line and other federally licensed infrastructure condemnations, where a broad preemption holding could invite condemnors to argue that state fee-shifting statutes no longer apply to them either. For commercial and agricultural landowners, developers with land banked along known utility corridors, and the counsel who represent them in condemnation proceedings, the case is worth tracking closely regardless of which side ultimately prevails. A ruling for WBI Energy would mean federally licensed pipeline condemnors need not reimburse a landowner's legal fees even when the landowner successfully increases the compensation award, meaningfully raising the practical cost of contesting a lowball valuation and likely pushing more owners to settle quickly rather than litigate, while a ruling for the Hoffmanns would preserve state fee-shifting protections in this context and, in states with landowner-friendly statutes, keep real pressure on condemnors to make credible initial offers. Either way, property owners anywhere along a proposed interstate pipeline route should factor the current fee-shifting uncertainty into their negotiating posture now and document litigation costs carefully if a dispute proceeds, since the decision will likely settle how this fee question is litigated nationwide for years to come.
live-087: Wilmington Trust National Association, acting as trustee for the commercial mortgage-backed securities trust holding the loan, filed a $25.4 million foreclosure lawsuit on August 14, 2026 in the Circuit Court of Cook County against Nakash Lincoln LLC and Lincoln 1816 LLC, entities controlled by the Nakash family, founders of the Jordache jeans empire. The target of the suit is Hotel Lincoln, a 184-room boutique property overlooking Lincoln Park Zoo at 1816 North Clark Street in Chicago. That pattern is what CMBS special servicers, bondholders, and workout counsel are watching closely across the broader lending market: sponsors who built diversified regional portfolios during the low-rate years of the last decade are now facing coordinated refinancing gaps as loans mature in a materially higher-rate environment, and a single sponsor's distress can surface as multiple, geographically unconnected foreclosure filings rather than one consolidated proceeding, since each loan sits in its own securitization silo with its own trustee and local counsel and no structural mechanism forces a unified resolution. For lenders and servicers evaluating a maturity default, the case underscores the value of treating a single missed payment as a potential window into a borrower's broader capital position rather than an isolated event, and of cross-referencing a sponsor's other holdings before agreeing to forbearance or modification terms that assume the distress is confined to one asset. It is also a reminder to owners of well-located, historically strong-performing hospitality and retail assets that an irreplaceable location does not insulate a loan from the current maturity wall, and that refinancing conversations are best started well before a maturity date rather than after a default has already been declared.
live-088: A New York-based developer has taken an unusually aggressive legal stance against a municipality's land-use apparatus, filing a federal complaint in late August 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida accusing the Town of Lake Park, Florida of corruption, blackmail, and extortion in connection with a stalled affordable housing project. When Alder declined, the complaint alleges, Baird directed a town code enforcement officer to issue 34 separate code violations against the properties, a volume Alder characterizes as retaliatory rather than the product of independently identified code deficiencies. The lawsuit seeks an injunction barring the town from imposing further code enforcement fines, an order compelling Lake Park to act on Alder's pending development applications rather than leave them in administrative limbo, and monetary damages for the harm the delay and citations have allegedly caused the project's economics. Baird has denied the allegations attributed to him and has characterized the lawsuit as retaliation against him and other town officials for performing their official duties. The case sits at the intersection of two doctrines commercial developers encounter far more often separately than together: the well-worn body of due process and equal protection case law governing municipal land-use decisions, under which developers regularly challenge permit denials and selective code enforcement as arbitrary, and the considerably rarer invocation of extortion and corruption theories against a sitting municipal attorney personally, framing enforcement as an instrument of an individually motivated scheme to force a below-market sale to a favored buyer. Proving that theory requires tying specific enforcement actions to the alleged quid pro quo, which is why the complaint leans heavily on the direct statements attributed to Baird rather than resting on the volume of citations alone, and Baird's potential immunity for acts taken in his official capacity will likely shape the case's trajectory before the underlying zoning issues are reached on the merits. For developers assembling sites for affordable or mixed-income housing in small municipalities, the case is a reminder that the same local discretion that makes density bonuses and housing incentives possible also concentrates significant, difficult-to-check power in a small number of local officials, leaving few fast or affordable remedies once that relationship turns adversarial short of federal litigation of exactly this kind. It counsels building a contemporaneous written record of every interaction with permitting and code enforcement officials from a project's earliest stages, particularly communications touching on alternative buyers or settlement overtures, since that documentation is what can transform an ordinary permitting dispute into a viable corruption or civil-rights claim, and it counsels weighing, before committing significant capital to an assemblage in a jurisdiction with limited institutional checks on a single official, whether the approval path realistically depends on the goodwill of one or two individuals rather than a more insulated, board-driven process.
live-089: A pair of Utah nonprofits, Kane Creek Development Watch and Living Rivers, filed suit on February 10, 2026 in Utah's Seventh District Court in Grand County against the Lieutenant Governor of Utah, who administers the certification process at issue, and against the developer behind Echo Canyon, a proposed 176-acre mixed-use resort development in the Kane Creek canyon corridor southwest of Moab along the Colorado River. The complaint asks the court to invalidate both Senate Bill 258, the 2024 statute that created Utah's 'preliminary municipality' designation, and the certification the law conferred on Echo Canyon as the state's first project to use it. SB258 lets landowners who control a qualifying parcel petition the Lieutenant Governor's office to certify a transitional governing board with authority to adopt zoning ordinances, approve infrastructure, and otherwise exercise land-use powers ordinarily reserved to elected county or city government, while the entity pursues a path toward formal incorporation as a town. Echo Canyon received that certification in June 2025, becoming the first project in the state to do so. Current plans for the site call for roughly 478 housing units, 102 overnight accommodations, and about 67,000 square feet of commercial space in a corridor that had otherwise been governed by Grand County's land-use code. The plaintiffs' central claim is constitutional: that SB258 transfers zoning and land-use authority to a board effectively selected by and answerable to the landowners seeking to develop the property, without an election, public vote, or the oversight mechanisms that ordinarily constrain a municipality's exercise of police power. The complaint separately argues the statute is an impermissible 'private or special' law under the Utah Constitution's bar on legislation that benefits a specific, identifiable private party rather than establishing a generally applicable rule, contending SB258's qualifying criteria fit only the Echo Canyon parcel at the time of passage. The governance challenge does not stand alone. The same two plaintiffs filed a related suit in mid-2025 challenging the water rights Echo Canyon's developer has claimed for the project, arguing several of the underlying rights, including one the plaintiffs say lapsed in 2019 after the developer missed a state filing deadline, have been forfeited through decades of nonuse and cannot lawfully support the scale of development now proposed. A hearing on motions to dismiss in that companion case was calendared for March 2026. Together, the two matters put both Echo Canyon's governing authority and its water supply before Utah courts at the same time. The case carries weight beyond Grand County. A small but growing number of states have experimented with statutory pathways letting large-scale developers exercise quasi-governmental land-use authority over their own projects, marketed as a way to accelerate housing and infrastructure delivery without waiting on traditional municipal approval processes. Utah's preliminary municipality law is among the most aggressive versions of that model now on the books, and a ruling on its constitutionality will shape how other states calibrate similar proposals and how far developers elsewhere can lean on self-governance structures to bypass friction with existing local government. The practical upshot for CRE developers and their counsel is that a governance structure built on novel, largely untested statutory authority should be treated as a live litigation risk rather than a closed entitlement question, with underwriting timelines built accordingly rather than assuming certification is the final word. Because the fight over Echo Canyon's governing authority is running alongside a separate water-rights forfeiture claim, sponsors of large resort or mixed-use projects in water-constrained jurisdictions should independently confirm that every underlying water right has been affirmatively put to beneficial use and well documented, since a forfeiture theory can sink a project's viability regardless of how the zoning dispute comes out. And because a successful constitutional challenge here could retroactively cloud title, permits, or entitlements issued while the certification was in effect, lenders and equity partners financing projects that rely on first-of-their-kind statutory structures should watch this litigation closely rather than treat the underlying law as settled.
live-090: A $40 million dispute between the developer of a Richmond riverfront apartment tower and the investment firm that bought it is now before the Richmond Circuit Court, testing how far a seller's post-closing repair promises can shield it from a fraud claim once the underlying defects turn out to run deeper than disclosed. Four Mile Capital, the Denver-based investment firm that paid nearly $50 million in 2021 for River's Edge at Manchester, a 212-unit riverfront apartment building at 505 Porter Street in Richmond, Virginia, is asking the court to let a fraud claim against the building's developer proceed to trial. The developer, Reynolds South Tower LLC, an entity associated with Guy Blundon of CMB Development and Mark Purcell of Purcell Construction Corp., is fighting to have that fraud count dismissed, arguing at an August 7 hearing that Four Mile was never misled about the condition of the building it bought. The dispute traces back to the 2021 sale itself. Four Mile has acknowledged it knew River's Edge had experienced water leaks before the sale closed, and that the sellers agreed, as part of the deal, to perform repairs both before and after closing. For roughly a year, that arrangement held, with repair work continuing into 2022. But Four Mile alleges that by 2022, Purcell had stopped making good on the repair commitment, and the leaks persisted. In 2023, after the water intrusion continued despite the earlier repairs, Four Mile hired an outside engineering firm to investigate the building envelope. That investigation, the complaint alleges, revealed that River's Edge was not built in accordance with its own architectural design, and specifically that the building lacked the waterproof sheathing Four Mile says it was told had been installed. First filed in Richmond Circuit Court in May 2025, the suit asserts fraud, breach of contract, negligence, and business conspiracy, and seeks more than $40 million in damages. The legal fight now centers on a distinction that separates ordinary construction-defect claims from fraud claims: whether a seller's affirmative misrepresentation about how a building was actually constructed, as opposed to a general failure to disclose a known defect, survives a motion to dismiss under Virginia law. Reynolds South Tower's attorney, Stephen Faraci of Whiteford, Taylor & Preston, argued that Four Mile was not misled about the state of the building, framing the pre-sale water leaks and subsequent repair arrangement as evidence that Four Mile bought the property with eyes open to its condition. Four Mile's attorney, Dylan Graham of the Fairfax-based Wise Law Firm, countered that the misrepresentations extended beyond the leaks Four Mile already knew about, to specific, verifiable claims about the building's underlying construction that a 2023 investigation showed were false. If Judge McClenney allows the fraud count to survive, the case will proceed toward discovery on the theory that a seller's repair commitments during and after a sale process do not necessarily cure, or waive, an underlying misrepresentation about how the asset was built in the first place, a sequence increasingly common in multifamily transactions where sellers negotiate a known-issue, ongoing-repair framework to keep a deal moving rather than disclosing the full scope of a defect before closing. A dismissal, by contrast, would reinforce the more buyer-protective baseline: that a purchaser who proceeds to close with actual knowledge of a defect assumes substantial risk that later-discovered aggravating facts will not resurrect a fraud theory once the deal is done. For buyers of existing multifamily assets, the case is a reminder to document precisely what representations a seller makes about the underlying cause and construction of a known defect whenever a repair commitment is negotiated in lieu of a price reduction or holdback, since a promise to fix the problem does not necessarily waive a later fraud claim if the seller's account of the defect's cause turns out to be false. Commissioning an independent forensic investigation promptly once negotiated repairs stall or fail to resolve a recurring issue can be decisive both for quantifying damages and for establishing that a construction-method misrepresentation, rather than merely a disclosed defect, is what is actually being litigated, and sellers extending post-closing repair support for a known issue should recognize that continuing that support, rather than disclosing its full scope up front, will not necessarily insulate them from fraud exposure if the underlying defect proves more extensive than represented at the time of sale.
live-091: New York-based Mack Real Estate Group asked a Colorado state court on September 4 to appoint an emergency, ex parte receiver over X Denver, the 12-story, 450-unit apartment complex at 3100 Inca Street in Denver's Ballpark neighborhood, alleging that the $170 million loan it made against the property has been in default since the note matured in January 2025. The filing seeks to place day-to-day control of the five-year-old building into the hands of a court-appointed receiver while the underlying debt dispute plays out, a remedy lenders increasingly favor over a slower foreclosure process when a borrower's ability to manage a distressed asset is itself in question. X Denver opened in 2021, developed by Chicago-based The X Co. as one of two X-branded apartment towers the developer built in Denver's Arapahoe Square and Ballpark submarkets during the city's last major multifamily construction wave. In January 2022, the property's then-owner secured the $170 million loan from Mack Real Estate Group to finance the completed asset, a debt load reflecting the aggressive underwriting many construction and bridge lenders extended to stabilized, newly delivered multifamily properties at the top of that cycle. According to Mack's filing, the loan reached its scheduled maturity in January 2025, and rather than being repaid or refinanced, the note has sat in default for roughly eight months without resolution. The current record ownership of X Denver is not entirely clear from public filings, a common feature of distressed assets that have passed through multiple special-servicing or workout arrangements since a loan's original closing. The case adds X Denver to a small but growing list of formerly marquee Denver multifamily and office assets now facing lender-driven receivership actions, following a similar filing weeks earlier by U.S. Bank National Association against the ownership of Republic Plaza, Denver's tallest office tower, after a second maturity default on that property's CMBS loan. Both cases illustrate a pattern playing out across gateway and secondary markets alike: lenders confronting a maturity default on a well-located, physically sound asset are increasingly bypassing extended forbearance negotiations in favor of an immediate receivership filing, particularly where a loan has already gone unresolved for months past maturity. An ex parte receivership request, as Mack has made here, asks the court to act before the borrower has had a full opportunity to respond, a procedural posture reserved for situations where a lender can show urgency, such as a risk that rents, security deposits, or other collateral proceeds might be dissipated or mismanaged absent immediate court supervision. For a 450-unit asset generating substantial monthly rental income, the practical effect of a receiver's appointment is significant well before any final adjudication of the underlying default: a court-appointed receiver typically takes over rent collection, vendor payments, and operating decisions immediately, effectively transferring functional control of the property away from ownership while litigation over the debt itself proceeds on a separate, usually slower track. That makes the receivership motion, rather than any eventual foreclosure judgment, the practical battleground in cases like this one, and borrowers facing an ex parte request typically have only a narrow window to contest the appointment or negotiate an alternative before a receiver is installed. Borrowers with loans approaching, or already past, a scheduled maturity date should not assume that a lender's silence in the months immediately following default reflects an intention to negotiate an extension or workout, since an extended post-maturity default period can instead be a lender building its record for exactly the kind of ex parte receivership motion filed here. Because such a request can be granted with limited advance notice, ownership entities carrying matured, unresolved CRE debt should have workout counsel and a response strategy in place well before a lender files, and with Denver now producing multiple lender-driven receivership actions against well-known, recently built assets in quick succession, owners and equity investors in the market's multifamily and office towers should treat a maturity default, even on an otherwise physically healthy property, as carrying meaningfully higher and faster litigation risk than it might have a few years ago.
live-092: A Miami-based special servicer has filed suit to foreclose on a suburban Chicago shopping center controlled by embattled Austin investor Nate Paul, seeking roughly $46 million after a loan workout the parties struck barely a year ago broke down. The action, filed in the Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois against WC MRP Calumet Center, LLC, adds another property to the long list of assets tied to Paul's World Class Holdings empire that have landed in foreclosure court, and it illustrates a pattern now recurring across the country's distressed CMBS market: loans that survive one round of forbearance are increasingly defaulting again once their reinstated terms come due. Rialto Capital Advisors, acting as special servicer for the trust holding the securitized loan, brought the complaint on behalf of the certificateholders that ultimately own the debt. The property at issue is a more than 159,000-square-foot retail center at 410-500 River Oaks West Road in Calumet City, Illinois, which the World Class-affiliated borrower acquired for $7.7 million in 2014. That acquisition was financed, and later refinanced, as part of a larger $38.3 million mortgage loan originated in 2015 by German American Capital Corporation and secured by a portfolio of World Class-owned shopping centers across the Midwest, later pooled into a CMBS trust that left loan administration and enforcement in Rialto's hands as special servicer. According to Rialto's complaint, the parties had already been through one cycle of distress on this loan. A reinstatement agreement, executed roughly a year before this suit, was meant to cure an earlier default and put the loan back on a performing footing. Instead, the borrowing entity defaulted again, prompting Rialto to move for foreclosure rather than pursue a second workout. The complaint also reflects the toll broader portfolio-level distress has taken on the underlying collateral: appraisals across the pooled shopping-center portfolio have fallen from a cumulative $56.6 million at origination to roughly $46.3 million more recently, even as the loan balance itself remains largely unchanged, leaving the lender materially under-collateralized relative to its original underwriting. The Calumet City filing cannot be separated from Paul's broader legal and financial history. Paul, the founder of World Class Holdings, was arrested in 2023 on charges that he falsified information to secure roughly $172 million in loans, and his real estate empire has already lost multiple Austin-area properties, collectively valued in the hundreds of millions of dollars, to foreclosure sales in recent years. The Calumet City action extends that pattern into the Midwest and signals that lenders holding World Class-linked paper are increasingly unwilling to extend further patience once a reinstated loan slips again. For CMBS investors, special servicers, and other CRE lenders, the case is a useful data point on how quickly patience erodes once a borrower with a documented history of loan trouble defaults a second time on the same collateral, and it underscores a theme playing out across the retail and multifamily sectors alike this year: portfolio-level cross-collateralization means that trouble at one asset, or a broader deterioration in a sponsor's overall financial condition, can put an entire regional portfolio at risk of enforcement even where an individual property is performing reasonably well on its own. Owners whose properties sit within a cross-collateralized loan pool should independently monitor co-borrowers' and guarantors' financial condition across the entire pool rather than just their own asset's performance, borrowers who have already been through one reinstatement should treat any subsequent shortfall as carrying materially higher foreclosure risk than a first-time default, and lenders evaluating new credit to sponsors with a track record of defaults elsewhere in their portfolio should weight that history heavily in underwriting and ongoing monitoring.
live-093: A federal magistrate judge in the Eastern District of Missouri has allowed investors in a stalled St. Peters, Missouri apartment project to file an amended fraud complaint against developer Jeffrey J. Tegethoff and his affiliated companies, keeping alive a civil securities and fraud suit that runs on a parallel track with Tegethoff Development's own Chapter 11 bankruptcy case. The ruling, issued by Magistrate Judge John M. Bodenhausen in Solera Multifamily, LLC v. Tegethoff, No. 4:25-CV-1877-JMB, stays the plaintiffs' claims against the now-bankrupt corporate defendants while permitting the case against Tegethoff individually and non-debtor affiliates to proceed, a procedural split commercial real estate investors should watch closely as similar sponsor-collapse litigation works through courts nationally. The underlying dispute traces to Old Hickory Village, a multifamily development in St. Peters that Tegethoff and his companies began in 2022. Plaintiffs Solera Multifamily, LLC and Hickory Investors, LLC allege they invested nearly $3 million in the project and that Tegethoff diverted those funds to purposes unrelated to the development, including personal expenses. According to the plaintiffs, the diversion left contractors on the project unpaid and caused significant construction delays, and other investors were reportedly forced to make additional capital contributions to keep the project moving, diluting the stakes of investors who had already put money in. The complaint, filed December 26, 2025, asserts breach of contract, breach of fiduciary duty, fraud in the inducement, state and federal securities fraud, theft and conversion, unjust enrichment, and a request for declaratory relief. Tegethoff has denied wrongdoing and moved to dismiss part of the federal case for lack of pleading particularity; Judge Bodenhausen's order allowing an amended complaint suggests the court was not yet persuaded dismissal was warranted on the existing record. The litigation landscape shifted further on June 1, 2026, when Tegethoff Development, LLC sought Chapter 11 protection in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Eastern District of Missouri, listing roughly $540 million in liabilities against a far smaller asset base, a filing that came as Tegethoff was simultaneously pursuing a separate, higher-profile venture: the roughly $500 million Oasis at Lakeport entertainment complex under construction at the Lake of the Ozarks. The bankruptcy filing automatically stayed the Solera plaintiffs' claims against the corporate debtor entities, which is why Judge Bodenhausen's order carves those defendants out while letting the case proceed against Tegethoff personally and non-debtor affiliates. In July 2026, creditors in the bankruptcy case escalated matters further, moving to appoint an independent Chapter 11 trustee and alleging Tegethoff engaged in insider transactions, provided inaccurate financial disclosures, and commingled corporate and personal assets, citing what the motion characterized as Tegethoff's own concession that he disregards corporate formalities between his entities. Taken together, the civil fraud suit, the bankruptcy filing, and the trustee motion paint a picture of a sponsor whose capital structure and corporate governance are under simultaneous attack on three fronts, a pattern increasingly familiar to investors in real estate syndications and closely held development ventures generally. The overlap between the civil fraud case and the Chapter 11 proceeding also illustrates a structural feature of bankruptcy law that catches many investor-plaintiffs by surprise: the automatic stay protecting a debtor from civil litigation reaches the corporate entities that filed for bankruptcy protection, but not necessarily an individual principal or non-debtor affiliate who did not file, which is exactly the distinction that let the Solera plaintiffs keep pursuing Tegethoff personally even while their claims against his company are paused. Investors who committed capital to closely held real estate development ventures structured around a single controlling principal should recognize that a sponsor's bankruptcy filing does not automatically halt fraud claims against that principal individually or against non-debtor affiliated entities, even where it stays claims against the bankrupt corporate defendants themselves. Creditors and investors evaluating a distressed sponsor's Chapter 11 case should pay close attention to allegations of commingled assets and disregarded corporate formalities, since those allegations, if substantiated, can support both a trustee motion in the bankruptcy case and a veil-piercing or personal-liability theory in parallel civil litigation, and developers and fund sponsors juggling multiple simultaneous projects financed by different investor pools should treat rigorous entity-by-entity financial separation as a legal necessity rather than an administrative formality, since a pattern of cross-project fund transfers is precisely the evidence both defrauded investors and bankruptcy creditors will look for once a project stalls.
live-094: Four small, longstanding businesses and a family that owns the building one of them leases are fighting to keep their locations on Brentwood, Missouri's Manchester Corridor, after the city designated a 75-parcel stretch of the road as blighted -- the legal predicate Missouri cities need to condemn private property and hand it to a developer. Represented by the national public-interest firm Institute for Justice, the plaintiffs -- National Feather-Craft Company (d/b/a Feather-Craft Fly Fishing), Time for Dinner LLC, Convergence Dance and Body Studio, and building owners Martin and Anthony George -- sued the City of Brentwood on December 12, 2023 in the Circuit Court of St. Louis County, arguing the blight finding was pretextual and that Missouri law bars using eminent domain solely for private economic development. The redevelopment plan at stake is substantial: in July 2023, Brentwood approved turning the Manchester Corridor over to private developer Green Street for a $436 million project including a three-story office building, a hotel, and a five-story multifamily structure, projected to generate $266 million in new revenue over 25 years. Brentwood's own blight report found 26 of the 75 parcels vacant and 48 showing "signs of physical deterioration" -- cracked parking lots, buildings needing paint, damaged trash enclosures -- which the city says is enough under Missouri's rule that an entire area can be blighted if a "preponderance" of it meets the standard, even where individual, well-maintained properties like the plaintiffs' do not. Following a four-day trial, Judge Kristine Allen Kerr ruled for the city in September 2025, holding that where "substantial evidence exists on both sides" of a blight determination, the question is "fairly debatable" and courts must defer to the city's legislative judgment rather than reweigh the evidence themselves. The plaintiffs argue that standard, if it stands, effectively immunizes any blight finding a city can support with cracked pavement or peeling paint on a fraction of a large district, regardless of how well-maintained the properties actually being taken are -- precisely the kind of blight-label abuse Missouri's Legislature intended to foreclose when it tightened the state's eminent domain statute in reaction to the U.S. Supreme Court's 2005 Kelo v. New London decision. Brentwood has separately defended the blight finding on flood-risk grounds tied to the Manchester Corridor's exposure to a 500-year flood event -- a rationale IJ's attorneys note sits awkwardly alongside the city's own recently completed $120 million Brentwood Bound project, which was built specifically to mitigate flooding and improve access along the same corridor. On September 26, 2025, IJ announced the plaintiffs will appeal, with attorney Bob Belden arguing the trial court applied the wrong standard of review and that, left uncorrected, the ruling threatens business and property owners anywhere in Missouri whose land a city wants to hand to a preferred private developer. For CRE owners, tenants, and lenders, the case underscores that a blight designation is not a formality to be ignored until eminent domain proceedings actually begin -- by the time a redevelopment plan and blight study are finalized, as this case shows, a court may defer heavily to the city's own findings rather than independently testing them. Businesses and owners inside any proposed redevelopment district should document their properties' condition proactively and understand that Missouri's 2006 reform, whatever its intent, may offer less practical protection against a determined city and developer than the statute's text suggests -- a live question this appeal should help resolve.
live-095: Regions Tower, the 36-story former Indiana National Bank headquarters a block from Monument Circle, is the subject of a $74.9 million foreclosure suit filed February 2, 2024 in Marion Superior Court by Wilmington Trust National Association, acting as trustee for a CMBS trust and through debt servicer KeyBank. The complaint names owner entities NG 211 N. Pennsylvania St LLC and Regions Tower MF LLC -- affiliates of New York-based The Nightingale Group, which bought the tower in 2014 for $65 million -- alleging they missed an October 1, 2023 deadline to pay off the loan in full. The 685,000-square-foot tower, designed by Dallas architect Thomas E. Stanley and completed in 1970, was roughly 75% leased at the time of filing according to building data cited in local reporting -- a level of occupancy that made the loan unable to refinance on its original terms even before accounting for the broader decline in downtown office valuations since 2020. Wilmington Trust's complaint asks the court to order immediate repayment of the outstanding balance plus accruing interest and fees, or in the alternative to foreclose and sell the property, and separately requests appointment of a receiver -- naming Riveron RTS LLC's Matthew Mason -- to manage the building during the litigation while keeping current manager JLL in place operationally. Regions Bank, despite lending its name to the building, is only a tenant and has no ownership stake -- a detail worth noting given how often building names outlive the entities associated with them once a property changes hands or falls into distress. Local commercial real estate economists quoted at the time of filing were already framing the case as part of a broader repositioning question facing aging downtown office towers: whether a building can be converted to multifamily, retail, or mixed use once its office economics no longer support its debt load, a decision Indiana University's Center for Real Estate Studies director Doug McCoy described as necessarily "building by building" rather than a one-size-fits-all answer. No further public update on the receivership or a completed sale had surfaced as of this writing -- foreclosure and receivership proceedings on a property this size commonly take well over a year to resolve, and the absence of subsequent news coverage is not itself evidence the matter has been resolved or dismissed. CRE owners and lenders should treat this as a live, pending matter to watch rather than a closed one. For lenders holding comparable legacy CBD office CMBS positions, the case is a reminder that a tenant roster in the 70-80% occupied range -- not obviously distressed on its face -- can still be enough to blow up a maturity refinancing once debt-service coverage and valuation assumptions from a pre-2020 underwriting no longer hold. Owners of similarly aged downtown towers should be stress-testing refinancing scenarios against current, not legacy, valuations well before a maturity date arrives.
live-096: A dispute over the former Willows Event Center site north of Broad Ripple, at 6729 Westfield Blvd., worked its way from a Metropolitan Development Commission approval to a courthouse settlement in barely six weeks. J.C. Hart Co., along with Chase Development and Evergreen LLC, sought to rezone 21.4 acres for "The Elements," a $61 million residential redevelopment along Spirit Lake. The Indianapolis MDC approved a 192-unit apartment and 16-townhome version of the plan in December 2023, sending it to the City-County Council for final approval. Before that vote, four plaintiffs -- Oxbow Estates Homeowners Association, Spirit Lake Co-owners Association, and property owners Thomas Durkin and Steve Yeager -- sued the MDC and the developer entities in Marion Superior Court on January 19, 2024, arguing the approved density violated a 2003 set of recorded covenants limiting the Spirit Lake area to 1.94 units per acre, enforceable by neighboring owners within 660 feet. The plaintiffs, represented by attorney John Kautzman, argued they were willing to accept meaningfully more density than the covenants technically allowed -- up to roughly 144 units -- but that 192 units plus 16 townhomes went too far. The dispute had a longer history than the lawsuit alone suggests: the development team first withdrew an earlier rezoning petition in June 2022, hours before a scheduled MDC hearing, before reviving a revised plan that the MDC ultimately approved in December 2023 -- the version the plaintiffs then sued over. That back-and-forth meant the project had already been scaled back once, from an original 2021 proposal of 256 apartments and 18 townhouses, before the covenant lawsuit forced a second round of cuts. With the City-County Council vote scheduled for February 5, 2024, the developer and neighborhood groups reached a settlement roughly twenty minutes into the Monday council meeting, following weekend negotiations: J.C. Hart agreed to drop to 168 apartments and eliminate the townhomes and condominiums entirely. The Council approved the revised plan unanimously, 24-0 with one abstention, and the lawsuit was dismissed with prejudice -- ending the litigation without a court ever ruling on whether the original density actually violated the 2003 covenants. For developers negotiating rezoning in areas with older recorded density covenants, the case shows that a credible covenant-enforcement lawsuit from an organized, well-represented neighborhood group can still force a real concession even at the eleventh hour before a final legislative vote -- here, a roughly 13% cut from the MDC-approved unit count and the complete elimination of the townhome component. Building negotiating room into an initial proposal, rather than treating Plan Commission or MDC approval as the last meaningful checkpoint, is the more efficient path to a project that actually gets built on schedule.
live-097: Fairlane Town Center, the enclosed regional mall developer A. Alfred Taubman opened in Dearborn on March 2, 1976, is under its second court-appointed receivership of the decade after owner Kohan Retail Investment Group defaulted on a $28 million loan.
